lesson.title: CH & G Clinic
lesson.subtitle: nacht, licht, recht versus goed, groen, geven

hook.title: Two Throat Sounds, Not One
hook.content: Dutch has a voiceless ch (nacht, licht, recht) and a voiced g (goed, groen, geven). English speakers hear both as 'a throat sound' at first; the difference is whether the voice is on.

pattern.title: Voice off, voice on
pattern.content: Put your hand on your throat: nacht has no buzz, goed does. The spelling helps: ch is usually voiceless, g usually voiced. A few words vary by region, but the contrast is real.
pattern.trap_note: Do not replace Dutch g with English g as in 'good'. Dutch g is a fricative, made with friction, not a stop.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (CH & G Clinic):
exercises.target_answer: de nacht, het licht, het recht, acht, goed, groen
exercises.meaning: night, light, right; law, eight, good, green
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "CH & G Clinic": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The night is long.”?
exercises.explanation: “De nacht is lang.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “CH & G Clinic”.

cues: The pattern: Voice off, voice on
It means: The light is green.
exercises.explanation: “Het licht is groen.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Voice off, voice on.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not replace Dutch g with English g as in 'good'. Dutch g is a fricative, made with friction, not a stop.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Je hebt recht.” is word-for-word “You have right.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Voice off, voice on.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The grass is green.
exercises.explanation: “Het gras is groen.” reuses only material taught in “CH & G Clinic” — Voice off, voice on.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het gras is groen.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Voice off, voice on.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “Eight books are big.”
twist.explanation: Acht keeps the voiceless ch; groot starts with the voiced g.

summary.outcome: Hear and produce the Dutch ch/g contrast without turning either into English g.
summary.takeaway: Two sounds that English lumps together become a visible contrast in Dutch.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: The Vowel Bridges.

nacht.etymology_derivation: English night and Dutch nacht are the same word.

licht.etymology_derivation: English light and Dutch licht are the same word.

recht.etymology_derivation: English right and Dutch recht are the same word.

acht.etymology_derivation: English eight and Dutch acht are the same word.

goed.etymology_derivation: English good and Dutch goed are the same word.

groen.etymology_derivation: English green and Dutch groen are the same word.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.
